tur53-3: The anterior cruciate ligament, the front one of the two ligaments that cross inside the knee, stops the shin bone sliding forward and the knee giving way when it twists. Most injuries happen without contact with anyone: stopping suddenly while running, turning the body while the foot is planted, or landing from a jump with the knee collapsing inwards.
tur53-4: The ligament can tear partly or completely; the meniscus and other ligaments can be damaged at the same time. The diagnosis is mostly made from your history and an examination; MRI helps confirm the diagnosis and see any accompanying injuries.
tur53-5: The diagnosis is made from your history and an examination. A meta-analysis combining 28 studies (JOSPT, 2006) compared the accuracy of the examination tests. These tests are carried out by a physician or physiotherapist.
tur53-7: With the knee slightly bent, the shin bone is pulled forwards. It picks up about 85% of tears (sensitivity) and is very likely to be negative when the ligament is intact (specificity 94%); the authors recommend it as the most valid test.
tur53-9: A positive result strongly supports a tear (specificity 98%), but it picks up only about a quarter of tears (sensitivity 24%); a negative result does not rule out a tear.
tur53-11: The anterior drawer test performs well in older injuries (sensitivity 92%, specificity 91%) but poorly in new injuries. MRI shows accompanying injuries such as damage to the meniscus and other ligaments.
tur53-12: This is why the decision is individual. Right after the injury it is not possible to say for certain who will do well without surgery; a few months of good rehabilitation helps make this clearer. Surgery is recommended more often for people who want to return to sports involving twisting and jumping, for those whose knee keeps giving way despite rehabilitation, and for those with accompanying injuries such as to the meniscus. You can make the decision together with your orthopaedic physician.
tur53-13: From stitching to reconstruction, from surgery to an individual decision
tur53-14: Over more than a century, anterior cruciate ligament surgery moved from stitching to reconstruction with a piece of tendon and to arthroscopy. Studies over the last fifteen years have shown that not every tear needs surgery and that measurement matters for return to sport.
tur53-15: Stark published a paper describing two patients with a cruciate ligament tear; both had been treated without surgery.
tur53-16: Mayo Robson carried out the first successful repair by stitching the torn cruciate ligaments to the thigh bone (published in 1903).
tur53-17: Hey-Groves described replacing the ligament with a piece taken from the sheet of tissue on the outer side of the thigh (fascia lata).
tur53-18: Jones described the method using the middle third of the kneecap tendon together with a piece of bone; it became the forerunner of today's bone-tendon-bone grafts.
tur53-19: As arthroscopy became widespread, the operation began to be done through small incisions.
tur53-20: A meta-analysis combining 28 studies (JOSPT): the Lachman test stood out as the most valid examination test for detecting an anterior cruciate ligament tear.

tur53-55: Tension-type and neck-related headache: types, diagnostic criteria, the effect of exercise and physiotherapy, a guideline comparison, a short history, warnings about painkillers and signs that need urgent attention. Six home exercises.
tur53-56: Headache is one of the most common health problems. In tension-type headache, the most common type, and in headache coming from the neck, exercise and physiotherapy aimed at the neck can reduce how often the pain occurs; for tension-type headache the evidence is more limited. Some headaches, however, need urgent assessment.
tur53-57: Tension-type headache is this much more common in women than in men
tur53-58: Headache on this many days a month or more, for more than 3 months, is considered chronic
tur53-59: Using painkillers for a long time and very often can make headache constant (chronic). In this case the medicines need to be reduced with a physician's support.
tur53-61: The type of headache is determined according to the International Headache Society classification (ICHD-3). A physician makes the diagnosis; the criteria below are to help you understand the differences between the types.
tur53-63: On average 1–14 days a month for more than 3 months, with at least 10 episodes; each episode lasts 30 minutes to 7 days. At least two of these four features: on both sides, pressing or tightening (not throbbing), mild or moderate intensity, not made worse by routine activities such as walking or climbing stairs. There is no nausea or vomiting; at most one of sensitivity to light or sound is present.
tur53-64: A neck disorder known to be able to cause headache, shown on examination or imaging, plus at least two of the following: the headache started together with the neck problem; the headache improves as the neck problem improves; neck movements are restricted and the headache is made clearly worse by provocative movements; the headache goes away after a diagnostic numbing injection (blockade) of a structure in the neck or its nerve.
tur53-65: Clues that help tell them apart
tur53-66: Pain that is always on the same side, the familiar headache being brought on by pressing on the neck muscles or by head movements, and pain spreading from the back of the head forwards suggest a neck-related headache; however, these features alone do not make the diagnosis.
tur53-67: In a study at 5 centres in Australia of 200 people with neck-related headache, both manual therapy and low-load exercises for muscle control of the neck and shoulder blade region, given over 6 weeks, significantly reduced how often and how severely headaches occurred compared with a control group; the effect was still present after 12 months.
tur53-69: The definitions of headache types have become clearer through the international classification; the place of exercise and manual therapy in neck-related headache has been shaped by studies over more than the last twenty years.
tur53-70: In a study of 200 people with neck-related headache (Spine), both 6 weeks of manual therapy and low-load exercises for muscle control of the neck and shoulder blade region reduced how often and how severely headaches occurred compared with a control group; the effect was still present after 12 months.
tur53-71: NICE, the body that issues national health guidelines in England, published its headache guideline: opioids were not recommended for tension-type headache; it stated that a course of up to 10 sessions of acupuncture may be offered for tension-type headache on 15 or more days a month.
tur53-72: The neck pain guideline of the Orthopaedic Section of the American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) (JOSPT): the place of exercise and manual therapy in neck pain with headache was defined.
tur53-73: The 3rd edition of the International Headache Society classification (ICHD-3) was published; the diagnostic criteria for tension-type and neck-related headache are based on this classification today.
tur53-74: A meta-analysis comparing types of exercise (J Pain): the effect of exercise in migraine and tension-type headache was examined; in tension-type headache, strength training reduced pain intensity, but the certainty of evidence was very low.

tur53-84: These exercises help strengthen and relax the neck and shoulder muscles, especially in tension-type and neck-related headache. Do the movements slowly and within a pain-free range; stop if you feel dizzy, get numbness spreading to the arms or a clear increase in headache. If you get double vision, blurred vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, numbness in the face, unsteadiness or nausea, stop immediately and see a physician. If you have recently had a blow to the head or neck, talk to a physician before starting the exercises.

tur53-86: Place your palm on your forehead. Without moving your head, push gently into your hand while your hand resists. Repeat for the back and both sides of your head. Using at most half of your strength is enough.
tur53-87: Sit on a chair with a low back and clasp your hands behind your neck. Lift your chest towards the ceiling to gently arch your upper back. Arch your back, not your neck; do not pull your head forwards with your hands.
tur53-88: Hold the edge of the chair you are sitting on with one hand. If you are holding with your right hand, slowly bring your left ear towards your left shoulder; feel a gentle stretch at the side of your neck. Do not lift your shoulder.
